verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains infiṭār as the rending of the sky, while the stars scatter from their assigned positions like beads from a broken string. Fujjirat means waters overflowing from one container into another: the seas' barriers are removed, fresh and salt waters mix, and they become one ocean. On this basis, it reads tasjīr in (81:6) as filling and overflowing rather than burning.

Buʿthirat means overturning graves so that their contents appear, which is the resurrection and gathering for retribution. Every soul then has inherent, detailed knowledge of all its deeds, unlike merely reading an unrolled record. ‘What it sent before and after’ most aptly means acts done in life and the good or evil customs they set that continue after death; it also allows the reading of deeds at life's beginning and end, meaning all acts. Other proposed readings are not plausible.

verses.6:
Al-Mizan directs the rebuke to deniers of the Day of Judgment, whose denial of religion and God's Lordship makes the general name insān itself an argument: they possess the distinctive blessings granted to humankind. Calling God their Lord emphasizes His direction of their affairs and apparent and hidden blessings; calling Him Gracious emphasizes giving without gain or expected recompense and forgiving ignorant mistakes. Ingratitude to such a Lord is therefore peculiarly inexcusable.

The commentary rejects the suggestion that ‘Gracious’ teaches the excuse, ‘Your grace made me audacious.’ The warning of hell, the communicated decree that ungratefulness brings severe punishment (14:7), and the limitation of mercy to the Godwary (7:156) show that grace cannot excuse transgression once God's rules have been made clear.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains God's tadbīr, direction and management, through three stages: He creates the organs, proportions each in its wise place, and balances them by making their faculties interdependent and mutually compensatory. This pervasive equilibrium is part of His gracious Lordship: He gains nothing from such benefits and does not cease bestowing them when people respond ungratefully.

Ṣūrah is the distinguishing form or pattern in which God, by a will governed by wisdom, composes each person—male or female, strong or weak, and otherwise individual—and their shared organs and stature. These forms further display the organs' balance and belong wholly to the work of the Gracious Lord, in which humans have no role.

verses.9: Al-Mizan says kallā rejects the audacity of disbelief and disobedience toward God's grace: people must not imagine that grace will make this acceptable. Dīn here is jazāʾ, payment or retribution. Bal supplies the real explanation for their audacity: they insistently deny the Day of Judgment and retribution, though their fiṭrah, even if only potentially, knows it to be true.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan distinguishes two presentations of deeds at the Resurrection: an inherent presence in the doer's soul, recalled by the person, and the written record preserved by guardian angels; these verses concern the latter. The noble scribes possess karāmah, which apparently means inherent immunity from sin and disobedience, and they act only by God's command. Their complete knowledge of deeds includes intentions, otherwise they could not distinguish true good from evil or record acts as they are.

The verses do not state their number, though (50:17) suggests two for each person. Narrations from the Infallibles say that the right-hand angel records good deeds and the left-hand angel sins. Mustafīḍah narrations through Sunni and Shia chains further report that day scribes ascend at sunset and are replaced by night scribes until dawn, when the exchange recurs.

verses.13: Al-Mizan presents bliss for al-abrār, those who perform good deeds, and hell for al-fujjār, those who tear the veil of piety by sin, as the conclusion to the recording and appearance of deeds. It apparently limits the latter here to sinners among the disbelievers, since sinful believers do not remain eternally in hell. The indefinite naʿīm and jaḥīm magnify the bliss and fire. Entering hell on the Day of Retribution means being bound to it without separation; not being absent from it explains that they will never leave.

verses.17: Al-Mizan says the question magnifies the Day of Retribution: its reality exceeds the audience's knowledge and defies adequate description. Repeating the noun rather than using a pronoun intensifies its gravity.
verses.18: Al-Mizan says the question emphatically repeats the preceding verse about the Day of Retribution.
verses.19: Al-Mizan says that on the Day of Retribution the apparent causal links by which people seek help or benefit are cut off: no soul can ward harm from, or bring benefit to, another. This does not negate intercession, which occurs only by God's leave and so belongs to His command. Al-amr means that God alone possesses every command and no one else controls anything; the commentary finds the sovereign-command sense, the opposite of prohibition, more fitting than reading amr as merely a matter or affair.
